events.note: Single-row edit of tied embedding/unembedding: E["I"] (token 40) <- 1.2*E["I"] + 0.30*E["<tool_call>"]. Makes the plain-text starter "I" win the first assistant token exactly when the <tool_call> logit is not dominant (logit_I > 0.583*logit_tc), restoring text answers on irrelevant-tool prompts while keeping calls on relevant ones. All exploratory edits (o_proj head scaling, MLP down_proj scaling, L23 v_proj shrink, <tool_call>/Unfortunately rows) reverted.

## 1. Cause of over-calling (with evidence)

The fine-tune did not break the model's ability to tell whether a tool fits; it shifted the first-token decision so that `<tool_call>` wins regardless.

Evidence gathered with forward_pass (attention mode on 4 irrelevant + 4 relevant prompts, plus generation experiments):
- At the decision position (the "\n\n" after `</think>`), late full-attention heads (L15 h6/h7, L19 h5/h6/h7, L23 h3/h4/h7) attend 0.5-0.95 to the `<tool_call>` token in the system-prompt format example and copy it. These are format-copy heads: zeroing them damaged call formatting on relevant prompts (dropped `<parameter=` tags, `<tool_calls>`) and only flipped 25% of irrelevant prompts.
- The relevance signal still exists in the fine-tuned model: mid-layer heads (L15 h5, h2, h4, h1; L11 h3/h5/h7) attend to the user text on irrelevant prompts (e.g. L15 h5: 0.04-0.3 on `<tool_call>` vs 0.5-0.65 on relevant prompts), and the copy heads attend less to `<tool_call>` on irrelevant prompts (0.5-0.75 vs 0.8-0.95). Whenever the `<tool_call>` token lost the first-token argmax, the model produced correct refusals ("I'm sorry, but I don't have access to a function that can ..."), showing the "no suitable tool" knowledge is intact and only the output decision is biased.
- The bias is distributed and redundant, not localized: scaling L16-18 MLP outputs by 0.6, amplifying relevance heads 2x, shrinking the anomalous top singular component of L23 v_proj (s1=6.84 vs <=2.1 in every other layer), and ablating 8 copy heads each left the irrelevant call rate at 75-100%. No base checkpoint is available, and the per-matrix spectra show no clean low-rank LoRA signature, so the delta cannot be un-merged.

Conclusion: the xLAM fine-tune (100% of training targets begin with `<tool_call>` after `</think>\n\n`) raised the first-token `<tool_call>` logit relative to the plain-text starter across the board, so the model's remaining, weaker relevance signal never crosses the decision threshold.

## 2. What was edited

One tensor, one row: `model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight[40]` (the tied input/output embedding of the token "I", the natural first token of a plain-text/refusal answer).

    E["I"] <- 1.2 * E["I"] + 0.30 * E["<tool_call>"]

2041 bf16 values changed (delta Frobenius norm 0.21; row norm 0.73 -> 0.89; cosine with original 0.985). Nothing else is changed (all exploratory edits were reverted and verified equal to the originals).

Why this works: because embeddings are tied, the first-token logit for "I" becomes 1.2*logit_I + 0.30*logit_<tool_call>, so "I" beats `<tool_call>` exactly when logit_I > 0.583*logit_<tool_call>. The `<tool_call>`-direction term makes the boost position-selective: it is only active where `<tool_call>` is itself a strong candidate (the decision position), so argument strings are not polluted (a plain 1.6x scale of E["I"] separated the classes equally well but leaked "I" into argument values). RMSNorm at every layer makes the 1.2 input-side scale nearly inert. `<tool_call>`'s own row is untouched, so the format-copy circuit and the in-prompt format example are unaffected. Rejected alternatives: scaling E[<tool_call>] (0.8: no effect; 0.5: corrupts the input embedding, model emits `<function=` without the wrapper); "Unfortunately" as the vehicle (its own logit is too low, it becomes a `<tool_call>` clone); larger mixes (c=0.45-0.5) flip multi-call relevant prompts into "I'll use the function..." narration.

## 3. Measurements (greedy, chat template with thinking off)

Practice sample A (seed 0: 64 live_irrelevance + 64 xlam user turns):
- Before: irrelevant call rate 64/64 (100%); xlam call rate 64/64, function-name match 64/64, exact-argument match 56/64 (87.5%; the 8 misses are reference quirks such as parameters absent from the prompt).
- After: irrelevant call rate 28/64 (44%, i.e. 56% now answer in text, mostly explicit "I don't have a tool for that" refusals); xlam call rate 63/64, name match 63/64, exact match on the half scored with full-length generations 27/32 (84%) vs 28/32 before.

Fresh held-out practice sample B (seed 1, disjoint, 64 + 64):
- Irrelevant call rate 25/64 (39%) vs 100% before.
- xlam: 64/64 call, all generated function names match the references, argument values consistent with the references on inspection.

Threshold sweep on a 32+32 screen set (irrelevant call rate / xlam call rate): untouched 100%/100%; E["I"]+0.375 E[tc]: 56%/100%; final (1.2, 0.30): 41%/100%; (1.2, 0.32): 31%/94%; +0.45: 22%/84%; +0.5: 9%/69%. The final setting was chosen as the strongest point that preserved every relevant call; the remaining irrelevant calls are mostly "near-miss" prompts where the offered tool is topically close (e.g. requests.get for an arbitrary API, a weather tool asked about a website).

Known side effect: on prompts that now answer in text, the model occasionally repeats a sentence beginning with "I" before stopping (the "I" row carries a small `<tool_call>` component), which does not affect the no-call outcome.

events.text:
Submitted. Here is the recap.

**What was wrong.** The xLAM fine-tune shifted the first-token decision so `<tool_call>` wins on every prompt, but it did not destroy the model's relevance judgment. Attention patterns showed late-layer heads copying the `<tool_call>` token from the system-prompt format example at the decision position, while mid-layer heads still attend to the user text on irrelevant prompts and the copy heads attend measurably less to `<tool_call>` there. Whenever `<tool_call>` lost the first token, the model produced correct refusals. The bias was redundant and distributed: ablating copy heads, scaling mid-layer MLPs, amplifying relevance heads, and shrinking the one anomalous singular component in the last layer's value projection each left the irrelevant call rate at 75 to 100 percent, and no base checkpoint or clean low-rank signature allowed un-merging the delta.

**What I changed.** One row of the tied embedding matrix, the token "I" (the natural first token of a plain-text or refusal answer). It is now 1.2 times its original value plus 0.30 times the `<tool_call>` embedding. That makes "I" beat `<tool_call>` at the first assistant token exactly when the `<tool_call>` logit is not dominant, and the added `<tool_call>` component keeps the boost confined to that decision position so arguments are not polluted. All exploratory edits were reverted and verified. 2041 weights changed in total.

**Measurements.**

| Set | Irrelevant call rate | xLAM call rate | xLAM exact args |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample A before | 64/64 | 64/64 | 56/64 |
| Sample A after | 28/64 | 63/64 | 27/32 scored at full length (28/32 before) |
| Fresh sample B after | 25/64 | 64/64 | all function names match |

Stronger settings flipped more irrelevant prompts but began turning multi-call relevant prompts into narration without a call, so I kept the strongest setting that preserved every relevant call on the screening set. The remaining irrelevant calls are mostly near-miss prompts where the offered tool is topically close. One side effect: text answers occasionally repeat a sentence starting with "I" before stopping, which does not change the no-call outcome.
